model-knowledge.note: Seed pending harvest; Wikipedia and vendor spec sources egress-blocked in this environment.

gaps: S-suffix (65W low-power) desktop SKUs are omitted across every generation. They are numerous (i7-2600S, i5-4570S, i7-8700S-class OEM parts, etc.), are near-duplicates of the 65W non-suffixed part at lower clocks, and are effectively absent from the retail gaming market. Roughly 60-80 SKUs not emitted.

T-suffix (35W) parts are only sampled, not enumerated: i7-3770T, i7-6700T, i7-7700T, i7-8700T, i9-9900T, i5-9400T, i5-10400T, i9-11900T. 12th/13th/14th gen and Arrow Lake T parts (12900T, 13900T, 14900T, 285T, 265T, 245T, 235T, 225T) are omitted because I am not confident in their individual base/boost clocks. Roughly 40 SKUs not emitted.

OEM-only / tray-only SKUs are omitted throughout (i5-8400T-class, i7-9700TE, i5-2405S, Core i5-13400T, the "Intel Processor 300/300T" Raptor Lake entry part, and the 65W OEM 12900/13900 variants already partly covered).

Celeron desktop parts are almost entirely omitted per the gaming-relevance filter. Only Celeron G6900 (Alder Lake) is included. Sandy through Comet Lake Celerons (G530, G1610, G1840, G3900, G3930, G4900, G5900) are not emitted.
Sandy Bridge and Ivy Bridge Pentium parts (G620, G840, G850, G860, G2020, G2120, G2130) are omitted: dual-core, no HT, no AVX, not credible gaming parts even in 2012.
Xeon parts excluded by remit, including the LGA1151/LGA1200 Xeon E-series that share silicon with the desktop i7 parts and were used in budget builds.
Alder Lake-N / Twin Lake (N100, N305) are omitted: BGA-only, not socketed desktop parts.
Core Ultra 200S T-variants and any 200S refresh SKUs launched after my knowledge cutoff are not represented.
uncertainties: HYBRID CONSISTENCY RULE CONFLICT — Arrow Lake-S (Core Ultra 200S) has no hyper-threading, so threads == cores. All 13 Arrow Lake records carry pCores/eCores and therefore violate the brief's "threads = pCores*2 + eCores" check (e.g. 285K: pCores 8, eCores 16, cores 24, threads 24, not 32). The topology data is correct; the validator rule needs an exemption for parts where hyper-threading is absent. Flagging rather than dropping pCores/eCores, which would lose real information.

AVX-512 on Alder Lake is emitted as FALSE for every 12th gen SKU. The honest position: Intel never validated or officially supported AVX-512 on any retail Alder Lake desktop part, but early C0-stepping silicon shipped with the unit physically present and several vendors exposed a BIOS switch that enabled it when the E-cores were disabled. Intel then fused it off in later steppings and removed the BIOS option via microcode from roughly early 2022. There is no per-SKU boundary I can state — it is a stepping-and-BIOS-date boundary, not a model-number boundary. Emitting false uniformly is the defensible choice; a build-specific override would be needed to model the early-silicon case.

LGA1700 officialMemMTs is the DDR5 figure only. Every LGA1700 part also supports DDR4-3200 on a DDR4 board, which the single scalar field cannot express. Consumers of officialMemMTs must read memoryType alongside it.

Skylake and Kaby Lake (LGA1151) memoryType is emitted as ["DDR4"] only. Both generations also officially support DDR3L-1600, and DDR3 H110/B150/B250 boards were sold. This is a deliberate simplification: pairing a 6600K with a standard 1.5V DDR3 kit is not supported, and the MemoryType enum cannot express "DDR3L". If the optimiser needs to model DDR3 Skylake boards this must be revisited.

l2CacheMB is null for i5-13400/13500/13600, i5-14400/14500/14600 and the F variants. These SKUs shipped from two different dies (Alder Lake C0 and Raptor Lake B0) with different L2 per core, and I cannot state a single figure with confidence. L3 for those parts is confident and is populated.

Arrow Lake non-K clocks (Ultra 9 285, Ultra 7 265/265F, Ultra 5 245/245F/235/225/225F) are null. Core counts, cache and TDP are confident; per-SKU base/boost frequencies are not. The existence of the Ultra 5 235 SKU specifically is my lowest-confidence SKU-level claim in the file.

processNm for 12th-14th gen is emitted as 10, i.e. the physical node behind the "Intel 7" marketing name (10nm Enhanced SuperFin). Arrow Lake is emitted as 3 for the TSMC N3B compute tile; its other tiles are on different nodes and are not represented.

tdpW for 12th gen onward is Processor Base Power (PBP), not Maximum Turbo Power (MTP). A 14900K is emitted at 125 W but draws up to 253 W. Any thermal or PSU sizing logic must not read this field as peak draw.

Broadwell-C (i7-5775C, i5-5675C) carries 128 MB of on-package eDRAM acting as an L4 victim cache. There is no field for it and vcache is emitted false because it is not stacked cache. This materially understates those two parts in cache-sensitive workloads — they behave far closer to an X3D part than their 6 MB L3 suggests.

igpuId slugs follow the ACTUAL ids in the sibling gpu-intel catalogue, which I read back and matched, not the "intel-uhd-graphics-770" convention my dispatch brief assumed. The sibling uses shorter ids (intel-uhd-770-adl, intel-hd-2000) and splits some parts by generation. 17 of 19 distinct references resolve exactly. Two do not, because the sibling seed has no record for them: intel-hd-4400 (Haswell HD 4400, referenced by i3-4130/4150/4160/4170) and intel-hd-610 (Kaby Lake HD 610, referenced by Pentium G4560). Those two are emitted as dangling references in the sibling naming scheme rather than as null, because null would falsely assert that those CPUs have no integrated graphics. The integrator must either add the two iGPU records or accept two unresolved joins.

Raptor Lake UHD 730 (i5-13400/14400, i3-13100/14100) points at intel-uhd-730-adl. The sibling catalogue split UHD 770 into -adl and -rpl records but created only one UHD 730 record for Alder Lake and one for Rocket Lake. Raptor Lake reuses the Alder Lake-S GT1 24 EU graphics, so -adl is the architecturally correct target, but the branding on those chips is Raptor Lake.

AVX2 is emitted false for pre-Alder-Lake Pentium and Celeron parts (G3258, G4400, G4560/4600/4620, G5400/5500/5600, G6400) — Intel fused AVX and AVX2 off on those. It is emitted true for Alder Lake G7400 and G6900, which I believe retained it; that pair is lower confidence than the rest.

9th gen X-series (Skylake-X Refresh) L3 figures for the i9-9920X/9900X/9820X and i7-9800X do not follow the clean 1.375 MB-per-core Skylake-X pattern because those parts enable extra cache slices on the HCC die. The values emitted are what I recall from launch coverage but are less certain than the 7000-series X figures.

Launch dates are month-precision ("YYYY-MM") and reflect announcement/availability as I recall it. Several 9th and 10th gen non-K parts were announced at CES and retailed months later; those carry the retail-availability month.

6th through 10th gen desktop parts all use Skylake cores at essentially unchanged IPC — Kaby Lake, Coffee Lake and Comet Lake are clock and core-count respins. The architecture field distinguishes them by marketing name, so any IPC model must not treat those four strings as four distinct architectures.
